The earthquake plan separates immediate protective actions during shaking from the deliberate post-event assessment and strict utility boundaries.

An earthquake plan needs two different decisions: how to protect yourself while the building is moving, and how to check for immediate danger after it stops. Trying to inspect the home during shaking adds risk. Trying to repair a utility or declare a structure safe afterward can do the same.
The
CDC during-earthquake guidance
and
USGS guidance
advise
Drop, Cover, and Hold On
. If you are indoors, stay there during the shaking. A doorway is not a universal safe place, and rushing toward stairs or outside exposes you to falling glass, masonry, furniture, and other debris.
Choose a safe action for the places you actually use
Walk through the ordinary locations where household members spend time: beds, desks, kitchen, living room, work area, garage, and any shared building space. Choose a nearby action that does not require crossing the room during shaking.
Starting place
Protective action during shaking
Important limit
Indoors near a sturdy table or desk
Drop, take cover under it, protect the head and neck, and hold on
Do not run outside or use an elevator while the building is shaking
Indoors without nearby cover
Drop near an interior wall or low furniture and cover the head and neck
Stay away from windows, exterior walls, tall furniture, and hanging objects when possible
In bed
Stay there and protect the head and neck with a pillow unless an immediate hazard requires moving
Broken glass and fallen objects may be on the floor after shaking
Outdoors
Move to an open area away from buildings, walls, trees, and power lines when it is safe to do so
Building exteriors and utility lines can shed debris
In a vehicle
Pull out of traffic, avoid overpasses and overhead hazards, set the parking brake, and stay inside until shaking stops
Resume driving cautiously; road surfaces, bridges, and approaches may be damaged
Adapt the position for mobility, balance, sensory, or care needs. A person using a wheelchair or walker may need to lock wheels, remain seated, bend forward if able, and protect the head and neck rather than transfer to the floor. Confirm individualized techniques with the person’s care or mobility team and practice without creating a fall.
If you are in a tsunami evacuation zone and you feel a strong or long earthquake, treat it as a natural tsunami warning. First protect yourself during the shaking; when it stops, leave the evacuation zone immediately by the locally designated route and move to high ground or inland. Do not wait for an alert. If you are on a beach or near the water, NWS says to move to high ground or inland after any earthquake as soon as you can safely do so. The
National Weather Service identifies strong or long earthquake shaking as a natural warning sign
;
FEMA advises moving high and inland after natural or official signs
. Save the local route before an earthquake, and avoid damaged or blocked paths. In the Pacific Northwest, USGS describes deep, Cascadia subduction-zone, and shallow crustal earthquakes as distinct regional sources; this context helps explain why a single “quake map” is not a household route plan. Washington residents can check the state’s
tsunami evacuation maps and route resources
; Oregon residents can use the
state tsunami viewer and map directory
. Coverage varies, and a route may be blocked after an earthquake. Follow current local emergency instructions.
Reduce what can fall before the next drill
During an ordinary maintenance window—not after an alert—look for items that could fall, slide, shatter, or block an exit:
tall bookcases, cabinets, televisions, mirrors, artwork, and hanging fixtures;
water heaters, fuel tanks, appliances, and equipment with rigid utility connections;
heavy objects stored above beds, seating, desks, pet areas, or mobility equipment;
glass containers, chemicals, tools, and breakable kitchen items;
exit doors, hallways, stairs, and accessible routes that stored items could block.
Move heavy objects to lower storage when practical. Use anchoring and restraint products only when they match the wall, furniture, appliance, fastener, lease, and local requirements. Gas appliances, fuel tanks, water heaters, masonry, chimneys, and structural retrofits need qualified review; a generic bracket or internet diagram is not a design.
Renters should document concerns and ask management which items the resident may secure. Apartment residents should also review the
small-space emergency plan
for stairs, elevators, alarms, and shared exits.
After shaking: check in an order that protects people first
Expect aftershocks. Keep sturdy shoes, a light, necessary mobility aids, and a way to receive official information reachable. If shaking begins again, Drop, Cover, and Hold On.
Check people and immediate danger.
Call 911 for fire, serious injury, entrapment, or another immediate threat. Give first aid only within your training.
Look and listen before moving.
Watch for fire, smoke, a gas odor or hissing, sparking, damaged wiring, broken glass, falling materials, and downed lines.
Use a safe exit if the building appears damaged.
Do not use an elevator. Move to the agreed open meeting place away from buildings and utility lines.
Account for the household.
Use the short message and out-of-area contact in the
emergency communication plan
.
Follow local inspections and re-entry instructions.
Do not enter a posted, visibly unstable, burning, or gas-affected building to retrieve belongings.
Treat damaged chimneys, leaning walls, shifted foundations, separated stairs, sagging floors or roofs, jammed doors, large new cracks, and fallen structural material as reasons to stay out and request a qualified evaluation. Appearance alone cannot prove that a home is safe.

Why it fits
A possible battery-powered way to hear local NOAA Weather Radio and supported emergency broadcasts. Verify reception and battery condition in advance; it does not predict aftershocks or guarantee service during an outage.
Key trade-off
A NOAA receiver only helps where the selected station can be received. Check local transmitter coverage, tune and test the radio at its intended location, and keep official alerts and other communication paths.

Apartment and high-rise: check the shared-building plan
If you live in an apartment or condominium, the resident may not control the building’s structural inspection, elevators, fire alarm, water booster pumps or shared gas service.
During shaking, remain indoors, move away from windows and exterior walls, and Drop, Cover, and Hold On. Do not run for a stairwell or elevator.
The
CDC’s current earthquake guidance
specifically addresses high-rise buildings and warns against using elevators.
When shaking stops, look for immediate danger from your current safe position. Use your building’s emergency instructions and directions from fire officials and responders. If you see structural damage, fire, a gas odor or a hazardous exit, do not assume a familiar stairwell is safe. Do not re-enter a damaged or restricted building until authorities allow it.

For building-wide power, water and access dependencies, keep the
high-rise power-outage guide
and
apartment emergency plan
available offline. Neither guide can replace a building’s current emergency plan.
Drinking water after shaking: an advisory comes before treatment
Earthquakes can damage water piping and service infrastructure.
Do not infer that the tap is safe because water still flows, or unsafe solely because the earthquake occurred.
Check the water utility, health department and building-management notices for your location.
CDC post-earthquake guidance
says to follow official local reports about water precautions and avoid potentially contaminated water for drinking, food preparation, teeth brushing and other affected uses.
If a boil-water notice applies
, follow the
issuing authority’s exact instructions
for water sources and uses.
If a do-not-drink or do-not-use notice applies
, do not assume boiling, a portable filter or household bleach makes the water safe. Chemical contamination and other hazards require the authority’s specified alternative.
If no status can be verified
, use previously stored, verified-safe water and contact the water utility or building manager rather than experimenting on a damaged system.
If pipes or well equipment may be damaged
, stay clear of flooded electrical areas and shared utility controls; arrange a licensed utility/plumbing or well inspection as appropriate.
Use the
emergency water treatment guide
for hazard-specific methods and the
water storage planner
for an independent stored-water reserve. A household filtration calculation does not certify water as safe following an earthquake.
Keep utility shutoff narrow and deliberate
Turning off every utility after every earthquake is not a safe universal rule. Controls may be damaged or inaccessible, and restoring service can require the utility or a qualified professional.
Gas or other fuel
USGS post-earthquake guidance
says to shut off the main gas valve
only when a leak is suspected
, such as from an odor or broken pipe. If gas may be leaking:
do not use matches, lighters, flames, switches, appliances, vehicles, or other possible ignition sources nearby;
leave the affected area and call 911 or the gas utility from a safe location;
use the valve only if the utility’s instructions apply to that exact service and it is safe to reach;
do not turn gas back on yourself after it has been shut off.
Propane, heating oil, and other fuel systems have different controls and hazards. Follow the supplier and fire department rather than applying a gas-meter instruction to another system.
Electricity
Damaged wiring, sparks, burning odors, heat, or water around electrical equipment can require disconnection, but approaching the panel may be unsafe. Do not touch wet equipment, downed lines, a damaged service entrance, or anything in contact with a line. Leave and contact emergency services or the utility when the route or equipment is unsafe. A qualified electrician should assess damaged wiring before reuse.
Water
A broken supply pipe can worsen damage. Learn the correct household and street-side controls in advance, but do not enter a damaged or flooded area to reach them. Street or utility-owned valves may be restricted. Ask the water utility or a plumber what the resident may operate and how service should be checked before restoration.
Do not let a checklist become a building inspection
FEMA’s Earthquake Safety at Home guide
helps residents notice hazards, but its checklists do not certify occupancy. Building officials, the fire department, utilities, insurers, landlords, structural engineers, electricians, plumbers, and other qualified professionals have different roles.
Photograph damage only from a safe location. Preserve receipts and notes for the insurer or landlord. Do not remove a posted notice, shore a structure, climb onto a damaged roof, enter a crawlspace, or move heavy debris to complete an inventory.
Phone readiness is a separate pre-event task:
the
ShakeAlert, MyShake and earthquake phone-alert guide
distinguishes USGS detection from MyShake, device features and WEA delivery. During shaking, take the protective action immediately whether or not an alert arrives.
Make the household drill short enough to repeat
Once a season or after a change in the home:
Call “earthquake” and practice Drop, Cover, and Hold On for one minute.
Check that everyone can reach the chosen position without crossing the room.
Name the open meeting place and out-of-area contact.
Point to utility controls without operating them and repeat the written shutoff boundary.
Identify one falling or exit-blocking hazard to correct during normal maintenance.
When running the drill, simulate the actual failure modes that a major earthquake introduces. Assume the power has failed and practice navigating the home at night using only the flashlight stored beneath the bed. Imagine the primary exit is blocked and identify a possible alternate route without entering or assessing a damaged area. If the drill reveals that a heavy mirror is hung directly over a sleeping position, that is a concrete physical mechanism of injury that must be mitigated by moving the object or securing it to wall studs with appropriate hardware.
A drill should also test post-event communication when local towers are overloaded. Do not assume cellular data will allow a video call or social media update. Send a simulated test text message to the designated out-of-state contact who serves as the communication hub for separated household members. If someone relies on a medical device, rehearse roles and confirm backup and relocation plans with the care team and supplier without interrupting the device. Follow their instructions for any equipment test.
Do not create real utility, ladder, lifting, or structural hazards for a drill. The useful outcome is a practiced protective action and a written decision about when the household leaves the problem to responders or qualified professionals. Never operate a gas valve during a drill, as doing so requires professional service to safely restart appliances. The drill must reinforce the strict boundary between identifying a potential gas smell or hissing sound and the physical action of shutting off the main valve only when those specific triggers are present.
Keep the drill, falling-hazard check, utility boundary, and meeting place on a private one-page paper record. Revisit it after moving furniture, changing care needs, or receiving new local guidance; use
My Household Plan
to review the fixed home-safety practice step. If the household includes pets or service animals, practice securing them with leashes or carriers, as frightened animals are a common complication during post-quake evacuations.
At coastal destinations, add a
local tsunami warning and evacuation-route plan
. Natural warning signs may require action before an official phone alert arrives.
Practice that route from the places household members actually use, such as home, work, school, or a regular care location. Use the local official map to identify the evacuation boundary, designated path, and safe destination; write down a second option only if local authorities identify one. Notice barriers such as stairs, gates, low crossings, or a route that depends on a bridge, then ask local emergency management or the property manager how to plan for them. If someone needs mobility or communication assistance, agree who helps and how to reach the destination before an event. Check the route again after local map or access changes. Do not walk into a closed area or use an unsafe route to rehearse; the map and current emergency instructions control.
Identify a falling hazard and check manufacturer, landlord, or qualified installer guidance before securing it.
Learn the utility’s gas shutoff instructions and when it is safe and appropriate to act; never restore gas yourself.
Keep a flashlight and sturdy shoes accessible near each occupied bed.
Practice Drop, Cover, and Hold On in primary living spaces.
Keep the household emergency contact number on a physical card.
